items.title: DeepInfer: high-performance, large-scale inference framework for DeepSeek models
items.headline: DeepSeek open-sources DeepInfer (Apache 2.0), its inference framework for V4.1-Flash on NVIDIA SM100 and Huawei Ascend 950
items.summary: DeepSeek released the inference framework behind its production services as an offline-inference engine. It currently supports only DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (default checkpoint V4.1-Flash-1017) on NVIDIA SM100 (CUDA 13) and Huawei Ascend 950 (CANN 9.2). It is built on DeepSeek's FlashMLA, DeepGEMM, DeepEP, TileKernels and DeepSelect plus custom TileLang kernels. Parallelism: attention data parallelism, balanced context parallelism and MoE expert parallelism with EPLB. Other features: DSpark draft-token decoding with confidence-scheduled verification, 'SWA bounded replay' (prefill runs only a bounded suffix of tokens through the decoder), asynchronous CPU scheduling, batch-invariant inference and deterministic sampling (NVIDIA only), and regex/JSON-schema/EBNF structured output.
items.result: The README shows prefill and decode throughput-vs-latency charts (4 SM100 GPUs for prefill, 64 for decode) but gives no numbers in its text. SiliconANGLE coverage quotes DeepSeek as saying DSpark cuts draft-token verification by about 30% for a 4-7% throughput gain, and that prefill compute is nearly halved; those figures are not in the README.
items.critique: This is not a complete serving stack. The README says the KV-cache system, prefill/decode disaggregation and load balancing across data-parallel replicas are not included, and press coverage says DeepSeek calls them tightly coupled to internal infrastructure. Hopper and older GPUs are not supported, so most existing clusters cannot run it. It supports one model. No head-to-head numbers against vLLM or SGLang are published, and all published benchmarks ran on NVIDIA hardware, so Ascend performance is unstated.

items.title: Introducing TorchTPU
items.headline: TorchTPU: native PyTorch backend for Google TPUs; reported Qwen3 235B MoE training at 1,828 TPS vs 1,937 for JAX/MaxText on 64 chips
items.summary: Google and Meta's PyTorch team describe TorchTPU, a native PyTorch device backend for TPUs rather than a JAX wrapper (unlike PyTorch/XLA and TorchAX). Code moves with model.to('tpu'). It offers three eager modes (Strict, Debug, and DeferAndFuse, which fuses deferred ops), and torch.compile(backend='tpu') compiles whole FX graphs to StableHLO through XLA. Collectives are implemented at the c10d Process Group level, so DDP, FSDP and DTensor work. Custom kernels come in through Pallas (with the Tokamax kernel library) and an experimental Helion path. About 450 ATen ops are supported, with vLLM/SGLang inference and TorchTitan training ports. The post says the repos open-source at the October 2026 PyTorch Conference.
items.result: Vendor-reported: Qwen3 235B MoE training at 1,828 TPS (PyTorch) vs 1,937 TPS (JAX/MaxText) on 64 chips, with weak scaling to 8,192 chips at 27.1-28.8% MFU. A single-chip TPUv7 30B prefill reaches about 25.7k TPS at 59% MFU (sequence length 5,120). DeferAndFuse is reported as 50%+ faster than Strict eager. On ~5,000 Hugging Face models, 98% run without crashing and 97% of a 657-model subset match GPU numerics.
items.critique: Almost all numbers are Google-run on chosen configurations. The InferenceX cost figure is a third-party SemiAnalysis benchmark, but the AgentX figure is Google's own. The default 'skinny' collectives cost 30-40% end to end. Dynamic shapes are forced off under torch.compile, so shape changes can trigger recompilation. FlexAttention is unsupported, and FP8/FP4 are still in development. The post names no license and is inconsistent about whether the code is already public.

items.title: Kronecker Delta Rule for Long Context Linear Attention
items.headline: KronLSTM: xLSTM-family linear attention with a Kronecker delta rule memory update; claimed to match or beat Gated DeltaNet at long context
items.summary: Delta-rule linear attention (DeltaNet, Gated DeltaNet) overwrites the matrix memory along the key direction, which can disturb other stored associations. KronLSTM instead revises the memory along a single rank-one key-value direction k_t v_t^T. Per the released code's README, it reads the current value y_t = k_t^T D_t S_{t-1} v_t for that pair (D_t is a gated diagonal decay) and writes S_t = D_t S_{t-1} + u_t k_t v_t^T, with u_t = beta*_t (c_t ||v_t||^2 - y_t). Here beta_t is an erase gate and c_t a write gate, and keys and queries are unit-norm. The authors show the memory dynamics form a Markov chain with a steady state and bounded expected norm, so no extra normalization is needed. Chunkwise (WY/UT form) Triton kernels are in flash-linear-attention. The release has four 1.5B checkpoints, pure KronLSTM and a 20+4 sliding-window-attention hybrid, each at 8K and 32K context, trained on 100B tokens.
items.result: The abstract claims KronLSTM is competitive with or better than existing linear-attention models, including (Gated) DeltaNet, especially on long-context benchmarks. This run could not read the paper body (arXiv rate-limited the HTML page), and neither the abstract nor the README gives numbers.
items.critique: No numbers could be verified, so the size of the gain over Gated DeltaNet is unknown. Scale is a single 1.5B / 100B-token setting. The README gives no throughput figures, only a command to benchmark the kernel against the KDA and GDN-2 kernels, so the cost of the extra read per step is unquantified. Kernels lack context parallelism and grouped value attention and use a fixed chunk length of 64.

items.title: MemT-1.0: Towards Memory-Native Evolution
items.headline: MemT-1.0 adds a Gated DeltaNet-2 memory to MoE backbones; reports 1.86x speedup and 66x less storage than a full KV cache at 128K
items.summary: MemTensor builds a fixed-size learned memory into the model instead of keeping the full history in the KV cache. Per the model card and repo, a Native Memory Block runs alongside backbone attention. It has a dynamic multi-channel memory matrix plus trainable memory projections with erase/write/forget/output gates, and its gated readout is added to the attention output. The memory is updated token by token at the end of each turn with a stabilized Gated DeltaNet-2 rule, and 'Mixture-of-Storage' scales capacity. Training is two-stage (continued pre-training, then post-training) on 34B tokens. Nano is built on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (451M trainable memory parameters). Flash is built on DeepSeek-V4-Flash (288B total, 17B active). Both are Apache 2.0.
items.result: At 128K history length, MemT-1.0-Nano reports about 1.86x end-to-end inference speedup and 66x less persistent storage than a full-context KV cache. On 11 memory benchmarks it beats other parametric-memory baselines on average and is reported as 'competitive' with retrieval-augmented methods.
items.critique: Benchmark scores appear only in figures. The text gives no numbers or named baselines for the RAG and full-context comparisons, and the repo admits textual-memory systems remain ahead, especially on long histories that need detailed evidence retrieval. The speedup is against the least efficient baseline (full KV cache), not against sparse attention or KV compression. The 34B-token adaptation budget and the training infrastructure are only briefly described.

items.title: Competing Learning in Hybrid Architectures
items.headline: In recurrent+attention hybrids, recurrence learns retrieval first and starves attention; freezing recurrent layers mid-training fixes it
items.summary: Hybrid LMs mix linear-time recurrent layers with softmax attention, expecting attention to handle in-context retrieval. Using layer attribution, the authors find a 'competing learning' effect: once one mixer type learns a function, the learning signal to the others is suppressed. Under typical data, modern recurrence learns retrieval faster than attention, so the attention layers never learn it. Their fix is staged pre-training that stops weight updates to the recurrent layers partway through training, so attention can learn retrieval.
items.result: On hybrids up to 1B parameters, the staged schedule is reported to substantially improve language-modeling loss, commonsense reasoning and a range of retrieval tasks across context lengths. The HF page gives no numbers, and this run could not read the code repo or paper body.
items.critique: Magnitudes could not be verified. The largest model is 1B, and whether the effect holds at the scale of production hybrids (Qwen-Next, Kimi Linear, Nemotron-H) is untested. The abstract does not say which recurrent mixers or attention ratios were tested, nor how sensitive the result is to when freezing starts. Freezing half the mixers could also cost capacity that a matched baseline would have to show.

items.title: TokenGate: Adapting LLMs for Fast and Memory-Efficient Prefill with Learned Token Pruning
items.headline: TokenGate learns which tokens to keep during long-context prefill; reports 1.4-11.3x faster TTFT and 1.5-3.4x lower peak memory
items.summary: TokenGate adapts a pretrained LLM to drop tokens early in long-context prefill. A learned gate with token-gated attention picks the tokens to keep, which avoids non-differentiable top-K selection during training. A released checkpoint shows the setup: on Qwen3.5-2B, the gate sits at layer 1 (a DeltaNet layer of the hybrid model) with a LoRA (r=16, q/v projections in all layers). It was trained on needle-in-a-haystack and is said to generalize to 32K-128K.
items.result: 1.4-11.3x faster time-to-first-token and 1.5-3.4x lower peak memory, with no reported accuracy loss on transformer models (truncated mirror summary).
items.critique: This rests on a truncated mirror summary plus model cards. The arXiv page was not readable (rate limited), so baselines (e.g. SnapKV, other prefill pruning) and benchmark coverage are unverified. Released checkpoints are task-specific (NIAH, MultiNews, 2WikiMQA, RepoBench) at 1.7-2B scale, which suggests per-task gates rather than one general gate. The wide speedup range likely depends heavily on context length and keep ratio.

items.title: ECHO: Efficient Causal Self-Recursion Beyond Auxiliary Multi-Token Prediction
items.headline: ECHO reuses the backbone's final layer for every multi-token-prediction horizon instead of auxiliary MTP modules, at half the overhead
items.summary: Auxiliary multi-token prediction (DeepSeek-style MTP) adds an extra module and forward pass per predicted horizon. ECHO, from Baidu's ernie-research, folds MTP into the autoregressive objective by running the backbone's own final layer recursively for each horizon. Dynamic Depth Sampling makes deeper horizons cheaper to train: per the repo, each step samples a depth D of 1, 2 or 3 with probabilities 0.6/0.3/0.1 (expected 1.5). The pretrained model can then serve as its own speculative-decoding drafter.
items.result: Per the GitHub README (step 78k, mean over 14 benchmarks): ECHO-1.5(3) scores 36.34 vs 35.38 for MTP-3 at about half MTP-3's training cost, and ECHO-1 scores 35.73 vs 35.22 for MTP-1 at equal cost. After one round of SFT, ECHO-1.5(3)-Instruct scores 37.88 vs 36.27 for MTP-Instruct.
items.critique: The gains are about 0.5-1.6 points, and the README admits that grading choices move scores by more than that: MMLU aggregation shifts 1.6-2.2 points, and dropping chain-of-thought on BBH changes one lead from +3.24 to +8.33. Five benchmarks use the eval platform's own numbers. The target model's size and the token count are not stated in the material read. Decode speedup appears only in the paper, and the repo's sglang path gives only a lower bound.

items.title: N-Gram Memories at Two Bits: Quantizing Lookup Tables in Large Language Models
items.headline: 2-bit quantization of n-gram memory tables in LLMs cuts output KL by 41-63% vs round-to-nearest, decoding only the rows a query needs
items.summary: Engram-style conditional-memory LLMs add huge n-gram lookup tables, which dominate parameter memory but are read sparsely. This paper's 'Conditional Program' stores the tables as independently decodable row records with short codes, local scales and a shared Gaussian trellis. Only the requested rows are reconstructed at lookup time, which suits offloaded or bandwidth-bound tables.
items.result: At 2 bits, output KL divergence is 41-63% lower than round-to-nearest quantization (truncated mirror summary). Further results were cut off in the source.
items.critique: Only a truncated summary could be read, so the host models, scale, downstream-task effects and lookup latency are unknown. Round-to-nearest is the weakest baseline. Comparisons against trellis/vector quantizers already used for LLM weights (QTIP-style) would be the meaningful test. Output KL alone does not show task accuracy is preserved.

items.title: Introducing TorchNeuron: Native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium
items.headline: TorchNeuron enters public beta: an Apache 2.0 native PyTorch backend that runs Trainium2/3 as a regular device, with eager and torch.compile
items.summary: AWS registers Trainium as a native PyTorch device through PrivateUse1 and torch.accelerator, so code moves with .to('neuron'). Eager mode runs ops immediately, with an experimental adaptive eager mode that fuses ops. In torch.compile, Dynamo and AOTAutograd graphs go through Torch-MLIR to StableHLO and then the Neuron compiler. FlexAttention is supported. Distributed support covers DDP, FSDP2, SimpleFSDP, TP/PP and DTensor, with collectives on Trainium's collective cores and EFA between nodes. Custom NKI kernels register as native PyTorch ops, and FlashAttention and MoE blockwise kernels are open-source. Public beta started 20 Oct (pip install torch-neuronx).
items.result: The only quantitative claim is from a customer: Deepgram reports about 60% more audio-seconds processed per dollar than its GPU baselines. No TorchNeuron throughput or latency is compared against a baseline.
items.critique: There are no first-party performance numbers. About 22K upstream PyTorch tests are skipped because their operators have no native Neuron lowering, and some models still fall back to CPU. The first release lacks dynamic/symbolic shapes, sparse tensors, NestedTensor, forward-mode AD, arbitrary attention masks and per-channel quantization. FP8 and TorchAO are private beta, and non-default streams share one hardware queue.

items.title: Diffusion at Scale: Introducing Mercury 3
items.headline: Inception releases Mercury 3 diffusion LLM via API: ~1,068 tokens/s on NVIDIA GPUs, 1M context, $0.20/$0.70 per M tokens
items.summary: Inception's third-generation diffusion language model, which generates by parallel denoising instead of token-by-token decoding, was published 19 Oct. The company says it has over 40x the total parameters of Mercury 1 (exact count undisclosed) and that context grows to 1M tokens from 260K in Mercury 2.5. It is available through Inception's API, OpenRouter, Baseten and Vercel with an OpenAI-compatible interface. Open weights are not mentioned.
items.result: About 1,068 output tokens/s on NVIDIA GPUs, which Inception says is 4-8x faster than comparison models. It claims to match or beat GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 'across a range of benchmarks' and to complete 50% of 50 live Mind2Web tasks.
items.critique: No per-benchmark scores, parameter count, GPU type or batch/concurrency settings are given, so the throughput claim cannot be compared to tuned autoregressive serving with speculative decoding. The model is closed, the architecture is undisclosed and nothing is independently verified. The 50-task Mind2Web sample is small.
